screens.title: Version Control with Git and Unity
screens.narratorSegment: In game development, version control is the guardrail that prevents lost work and confusing team conflicts. In this lesson you will learn why a distributed system like Git is the industry standard, and how it gives each developer a full copy of the project's history so work can continue even offline. We'll show the core commands you need to initialize a repository, stage changes, create clear commits, and inspect history. You will also learn Unity-specific setup: a proper. gitignore to avoid committing generated folders like Library, and Git LFS to handle large binary assets without inflating repository size. We'll cover branching so you can work on features without destabilizing the main build, and practical approaches for scene merge conflicts that Unity tends to produce. Throughout, you'll see concrete terminal commands and a hands-on activity to set up a new Unity project with Git and LFS. By the end you'll know how to protect your work, share it with teammates, and keep your repository lean and mergeable. What part of your current workflow could benefit most from version control?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Version Control with Git and Unity
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Version Control with Git and Unity

Protect history, collaborate across teams, and manage large Unity assets without bloating your repository. This lesson shows practical commands, a Unity .gitignore, and LFS setup so your team stays productive.

In this lesson
Initialize Git, commit changes, and use Git LFS.
Coming up
Configure .gitignore and typical branching flows.
Hands-on
Walk through initializing a Unity project with Git and LFS.
Visual Overview
Git Repository

A distributed history every developer clones. Stores commits, branches, and tags.

Commands: git init · git add · git commit
Unity Assets & LFS

Large binaries should be tracked with Git LFS to avoid repository bloat and slow operations.

Commands: git lfs install · git lfs track
Quick Terminal Cheatsheet
git init
git add .
git commit -m "Initial Unity project setup"
git lfs install
git lfs track "*.unity" "*.prefab" "*.png"
Follow the hands-on activity later to try these commands in a sample Unity project. The .gitignore and LFS steps are essential to avoid tracking generated files and to manage large assets efficiently.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain why version control is essential for team-based game development, perform the core Git commands to record and inspect work, and configure Git for Unity projects with a correct. gitignore. You will also understand how to use Git LFS to manage large binary assets so your repository stays small and fast. Finally, you'll be able to create feature branches and merge them back into a stable main branch while recognizing how to handle difficult Unity scene conflicts. These skills matter because they reduce lost time, prevent corrupted projects, and make collaboration reliable. For example, initializing a repository and committing incremental changes means you can always roll back a broken change instead of rebuilding from scratch. A common misconception is that Git is only for programmers; in Unity teams artists and designers benefit equally from clear versioning. Each objective includes a verified competency milestone so you know when you have demonstrated the skill in a real project environment.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Objectives: Troubleshooting & Collaboration

Troubleshooting and Collaboration Objectives

Practical remedies for common Unity Git problems and predictable collaboration patterns.

Diagnosis
Find the root cause

Use git status, inspect commit history, and identify whether generated folders were committed by mistake.

Remedy
Fix repository issues

Remove unwanted tracked folders, add them to .gitignore, and use Git LFS to move large assets off history where needed.

Coordination
Avoid scene conflicts

Coordinate who edits complex scene files. Prefer one editor per scene when possible and commit frequently to reduce overlapping changes.

screens.title: Why Version Control Matters for Game Development
screens.narratorSegment: A Version Control System records how files change over time so you can recover earlier states and understand who made which changes. In Unity game development this is essential because projects combine text scripts with large binaries and many people can touch the same project. Git is a distributed VCS: every clone contains the full history, which means developers can work offline and still commit local snapshots. This reduces risk—if a build breaks, you can roll back to a previous commit rather than rebuild the entire scene from memory. A concrete example: if an artist accidentally overwrites a material, you can restore the previous material file from Git history. A common misconception is that version control only benefits programmers. In reality, artists, level designers, and technical artists all gain from consistent history and branching strategies. Another pitfall is assuming Git will manage large binary files efficiently by default; without Git LFS those binaries inflate history and slow every clone. The core takeaway is that Git makes collaboration explicit and reversible: you can experiment on branches, test locally, and merge only stable work back into the main branch. How might a branching approach change how your team coordinates scene edits?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Why Version Control Matters
Core Concept

Why VCS matters

Version control records changes so teams can experiment safely, revert mistakes, and collaborate in parallel.

Key benefits
  • Recover previous versions after mistakes.
  • Branch to isolate features and avoid breaking main builds.
  • Track who changed what and why with clear commit messages.
Concrete example

An artist overwrites a material. Use git log to find the last good commit and restore the file, avoiding rework.

Common mistake

Assuming Git handles large binaries well—without LFS the repository history will balloon and clones become slow.

Analogy

Think of Git as a robust time machine for your project. Each commit is a snapshot you can return to, and branches are parallel timelines you can merge when ready.

Quick commands
git init
git status
git add .
git commit -m "Descriptive message"
git log
Key Takeaway

Version control prevents lost work and enables parallel development. Treat commits and branches as communication tools for your team.

screens.title: Core Git Workflow: Init, Stage, Commit, Inspect
screens.narratorSegment: A simple, repeatable Git workflow makes saving work predictable. Start by initializing a repository in your project root using git init; this creates the hidden metadata Git needs. As you change C# scripts, scenes, or assets, run git status to see modified and untracked files. Staging with git add selects the items you want to include in the next snapshot; use git add. to stage all changes in the current directory or target specific files when you want finer control. Commit staged changes with git commit -m "Your descriptive message". Good commit messages describe what changed and why; they are the project memory that helps teammates understand intent. After committing, use git log to review history and git diff between commits to inspect exact changes. A concrete example: after creating a PlayerAbility. cs and updating a scene, run git add PlayerAbility. cs GameScene. unity PlayerPrefab. prefab && git commit -m "Add player ability and prefab". A common mistake is trying to commit without staging; git commit will have nothing to snapshot. Frequent, small commits make it easier to bisect regressions and communicate progress to your team. How would you choose between staging individual files versus git add. in a busy sprint?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Core Git Workflow
Process Flow

Init → Stage → Commit → Inspect

Step 1 — Initialize

Run git init in the project root to create the .git folder that holds history.

Step 2 — Inspect

Use git status to see what changed and decide what to stage.

Step 3 — Stage & Commit

git add then git commit -m with a descriptive message. Small commits are easier to review and revert.

Example sequence shown on the right mirrors the terminal you will use in the hands-on activity.
Terminal Example
# initialize repository
git init

# check changes
git status

# stage and commit all changes
git add .
git commit -m "Initial Unity project setup with Git LFS"

# inspect history
git log --oneline
Key Takeaway

Stage intentionally, commit frequently, and use history to diagnose regressions quickly.

screens.title: Staging: What it Is and Why It Helps
screens.narratorSegment: Staging is the step where you choose which changes will be recorded in the next commit. Git's staging area, often called the index, acts like a photo frame: you place only the items you want to capture. This is important because you may have unrelated changes in your working directory—say adjustments to a shader and a new test script—and you want to record them as separate commits with clear intent. For example, use git add PlayerController. cs to stage a single script, then git commit -m "Refactor player movement". Clear, focused commits make it easier to review history and revert if necessary. A common mistake is using git add. indiscriminately, which bundles unrelated edits into one commit and obscures why changes were made. Another misconception is thinking staging is optional; while you can commit with -a in some cases, explicit staging encourages discipline. When working in teams, disciplined staging and descriptive messages are the currency of good collaboration: they communicate intent and make merges simpler. Try forming a habit of staging logically-related changes and write commit messages that answer what changed and why.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Staging: What it Is
Definition

The staging area (index)

An intermediate place where you prepare changes to include in the next commit. It helps you create focused, reviewable commits.

Why stage?
  • Group related edits into a single commit.
  • Avoid bundling unrelated fixes together.
  • Make history easier to understand and revert.
Example
git add PlayerController.cs
git commit -m "Refactor player movement to support sprinting"
Common mistakes & pro tip
Pitfall

Using git add . by default bundles unrelated edits. This makes future reviews and reverts harder.

Pro tip

Stage logically grouped changes and write commit messages that explain both what changed and why.

Key Takeaway

Staging is a planning step. Use it to craft commits that are easy to review and revert.

screens.title: Configure .gitignore for Unity Projects
screens.narratorSegment: A proper. gitignore is the foundation of a healthy Unity repository. Unity generates folders such as Library, Temp, and Obj that contain cached and user-specific data. These folders should never be tracked because they are machine-specific, large, and can cause conflicts. A typical. gitignore for Unity includes rules to ignore /[Ll]ibrary/, /[Tt]emp/, /[Oo]bj/, /[Bb]uild/, and logs, plus IDE files like. sln and. csproj. The chapter includes a sample. gitignore and a large list of Unity and editor-specific patterns you should include. Create the. gitignore in the project root before making your first commit so generated files never enter history. A misconception is treating. gitignore as a cleanup tool after files are already committed; once tracked, adding a file to. gitignore will not remove it from history. The correct remedy is to remove the tracked file and commit that removal, then push the updated history. This prevents future clones from pulling unwanted generated content. In short: set up. gitignore early, include common Unity ignores, and verify with git status before your first commit. Configure .gitignore for Unity Projects means add unity-generated and user-specific folders to .gitignore before the first commit to prevent conflicts and bloat.. In practical terms, avoid committing generated folders and user-specific files. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Configure .gitignore
Definition

What to ignore for Unity

Ignore generated and user-specific files so only source and essential assets are tracked.

Key entries
  • /[Ll]ibrary/
  • /[Tt]emp/
  • /[Oo]bj/
  • /[Bb]uild/ and /[Bb]uilds/
  • IDE files: *.csproj, *.sln, .vs/
Why it matters

Tracking generated folders causes conflicts and large repository sizes. Set this file early to keep history clean.

Sample .gitignore excerpt
# Unity generated
/[Ll]ibrary/
/[Tt]emp/
/[Oo]bj/
/[Bb]uild/
/[Ll]ogs/

# Visual Studio
.vs/
*.csproj
*.sln
If you already committed an ignored folder, remove it from tracking with git rm --cached and commit the removal, then ensure .gitignore prevents future tracking.
Common misconception

Adding entries to .gitignore does not remove files already tracked. Remove them from tracking and commit the result.

screens.title: Git Large File Storage (Git LFS)
screens.narratorSegment: Git stores each version of every file in history. That model works well for text but becomes problematic for large binary files common in Unity projects: textures, models, audio, and prefabs. Git LFS is a Git extension that replaces the file contents in the repository with small text pointers and stores the actual binary data on a remote LFS server. To use it, install Git LFS on your machine, run git lfs install in the repository, and then track file patterns, for example git lfs track "*. unity" "*. prefab" "*. png". This creates a. gitattributes file telling Git which files are handled by LFS. After tracking, add and commit as usual; LFS stores the binaries outside the normal Git object store. A frequent mistake is forgetting to enable LFS before adding large assets; those files then enter regular history and are hard to move out. Another misconception is that LFS eliminates the need to be selective about assets; you still should avoid adding unnecessary large files. Practically, use LFS for common Unity file types and verify using git lfs track. The hands-on activity walks through these commands so you can see the pointer files in diffs and confirm the binary content is managed by LFS.

keyIdea.text: Git LFS stores large binaries off the main Git object store and keeps pointer files in the repo, preventing history bloat.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Git LFS
Definition

What Git LFS does

Replaces tracked large files with pointers in Git history and stores real content on an LFS server.

Setup steps
git lfs install
git lfs track "*.unity" "*.prefab" "*.png"
git add .gitattributes
git add 
git commit -m "Track Unity binaries with Git LFS"
Practical notes
Verify tracking

Run git lfs track to list patterns. After commits, diffs show small pointer text instead of full binary content.

Common error

Adding large binaries before enabling LFS stores them in normal history. To fix this you must remove and re-add them after LFS is enabled.

Key Takeaway

Enable Git LFS early and track common Unity binary types to keep clones fast and history manageable.

screens.title: Branching and Merging Strategies
screens.narratorSegment: Branching creates isolated lines of development so you can build features or fix bugs without changing the stable main branch. A typical flow is to branch from main with git branch feature-name and switch to it with git checkout feature-name (or git switch feature-name). Work and commit on the branch, then merge back into main when the feature is complete and tested. This protects the main branch as a deployable baseline. For teams, a common practice is to create short-lived feature branches and merge frequently to avoid long-lived divergence. When merging, git merge feature-name tries to reconcile changes automatically. Source files like C# scripts are usually mergeable as text, but Unity scene files are often binary and cause difficult conflicts. The practical approach is communication: coordinate who edits a scene, lock scenes if your toolchain supports it, or assign one owner per complex scene to avoid simultaneous edits. If a merge conflict occurs in a scene file, consider accepting one version and manually re-implementing changes inside Unity, since hand-editing a scene file is error-prone. The key is frequent pushes and clear, atomic commits that make merges smaller and easier to resolve. How will your team structure branch lifetime to reduce integration pain?

keyIdea.text: Use feature branches for isolated work, merge frequently, and protect main as the stable baseline to reduce integration conflicts.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Branching & Merging
Process Flow

Feature branches and merges

  1. Create branch: git branch feature-name
  2. Switch: git checkout feature-name
  3. Commit work frequently on the branch
  4. Merge: git checkout main && git merge feature-name
Best practice

Keep branches short-lived and merge frequently to reduce conflict scope and simplify code review.

Merging Unity scenes

Unity scene files are often not human-mergeable. Coordinate edits or assign a single owner for complex scenes.

When conflicts happen

Prefer re-applying the missing changes inside the Unity editor rather than hand-editing the raw scene file.

Coordination tip

Communicate who is editing scenes and commit small increments to make merges manageable.

Key Takeaway

Branch often, merge often, and coordinate scene edits to keep integration smooth.

screens.title: Text Files vs Binary Unity Files
screens.narratorSegment: Git handles plain text files and binary files very differently. C# scripts are text files, so Git can show line-by-line diffs and merge changes from different developers automatically most of the time. This is why collaborative code editing usually scales well. By contrast, many Unity file formats such as. unity scene files and certain prefabs are binary or structured in ways that are not human-friendly. When two developers edit the same scene, Git may not be able to merge changes automatically, resulting in a merge conflict that is difficult to resolve by hand. The recommended approach is to prevent simultaneous edits to the same scene by communicating or shifting work to separate scene parts. If a conflict occurs, accept one version and re-implement the missing pieces within Unity, or use an external Unity-aware merge tool if available. A practical example: two developers edit camera positions in the same scene and cause a conflict—coordinate to avoid this or reapply the smaller change in the editor. Remember that Git LFS helps with storage but does not change merge behavior for binary formats. The takeaway: use Git's strengths for text, and adjust your team process to manage Unity binaries.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Text vs Binary
Comparison

Scripts (text) vs Scenes/Assets (binary)

Text files

Line-by-line diffs and automatic merges are common. Use git log and git diff to review changes.

Binary files

Scenes and many asset files may not merge well. Conflicts often need manual reapplication inside Unity.

Practical guidance
  • Coordinate who edits complex scenes at a time.
  • Prefer modular scenes or prefabs to reduce overlap.
  • Use Git LFS to store binaries but still plan for merge policies.
Example scenario

If two team members change the same scene, prefer one person's version and reapply the other's changes inside Unity rather than editing the raw scene file by hand.

Key Takeaway

Leverage Git for text merges; manage binary assets through team process and LFS storage.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and How to Prevent Them
screens.narratorSegment: Unity projects commonly suffer from a handful of version-control mistakes that are both easy to make and painful to fix. The most frequent is committing the Library folder. This folder contains machine-specific cached data and causes constant conflicts across developers. The simple prevention is to add /[Ll]ibrary/ to. gitignore before committing. Another recurring error is forgetting Git LFS for large assets such as textures, models, and audio. Without LFS each binary version stays in the repository and quickly inflates clones and operations. Enable LFS early and track common Unity types like. unity,. prefab,. png, and. fbx. A third issue is attempting to manually merge binary scene files; hand-editing scene files is error-prone. Instead, coordinate edits and reapply changes inside Unity when necessary. Practical remediation when mistakes happen: remove the tracked folder with git rm --cached, commit the removal, and then add the appropriate. gitignore entries. For large binaries already in history, consider repository migration tools or accept the cost of reinitializing a new repo after moving assets to LFS. The central message is preventative setup—. gitignore and LFS—combined with team coordination will avoid most headaches.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Common Mistakes

Top mistakes

  • Committing Library/ and other generated folders.
  • Not using Git LFS for large Unity binaries.
  • Attempting to hand-merge binary scene files.
Quick fixes

Remove tracked generated folders with git rm --cached, commit the removal, then add .gitignore and push. Re-add assets under LFS after track and install.

Team practices to avoid problems
  • Set up .gitignore and LFS before the first commit.
  • Coordinate scene edits and assign ownership when possible.
  • Commit small, descriptive snapshots and push regularly.
Key Takeaway

Early, deliberate setup and team coordination prevent most Unity Git headaches.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Hands-on: Initialize

Terminal-first setup

Follow these commands in your project root (the folder containing Assets and ProjectSettings).

Commands
# initialize repository
cd /path/to/GitUnityPractice
git init

# create .gitignore (add entries like /[Ll]ibrary/)

# install and enable LFS
git lfs install

# track common Unity binaries
git lfs track "*.unity" "*.prefab" "*.png"

# stage and commit
git add .
git commit -m "Initial Unity project setup with Git LFS"
Verification
  • Confirm .gitattributes was committed after git lfs track.
  • Use git lfs track to list tracked patterns.
  • In Unity, add a texture and verify git status shows the asset tracked by LFS pointer.
Key Takeaway

Complete the setup before working so generated files never enter history and LFS manages large binaries.

fullNarratorScript:
In game development, version control is the guardrail that prevents lost work and confusing team conflicts. In this lesson you will learn why a distributed system like Git is the industry standard, and how it gives each developer a full copy of the project's history so work can continue even offline. We'll show the core commands you need to initialize a repository, stage changes, create clear commits, and inspect history. You will also learn Unity-specific setup: a proper. gitignore to avoid committing generated folders like Library, and Git LFS to handle large binary assets without inflating repository size. We'll cover branching so you can work on features without destabilizing the main build, and practical approaches for scene merge conflicts that Unity tends to produce. Throughout, you'll see concrete terminal commands and a hands-on activity to set up a new Unity project with Git and LFS. By the end you'll know how to protect your work, share it with teammates, and keep your repository lean and mergeable. What part of your current workflow could benefit most from version control?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain why version control is essential for team-based game development, perform the core Git commands to record and inspect work, and configure Git for Unity projects with a correct. gitignore. You will also understand how to use Git LFS to manage large binary assets so your repository stays small and fast. Finally, you'll be able to create feature branches and merge them back into a stable main branch while recognizing how to handle difficult Unity scene conflicts. These skills matter because they reduce lost time, prevent corrupted projects, and make collaboration reliable. For example, initializing a repository and committing incremental changes means you can always roll back a broken change instead of rebuilding from scratch. A common misconception is that Git is only for programmers; in Unity teams artists and designers benefit equally from clear versioning. Each objective includes a verified competency milestone so you know when you have demonstrated the skill in a real project environment.

This second objectives slide focuses on troubleshooting and collaboration practices you will master. You will identify common version control mistakes seen in Unity projects, such as committing the Library folder or failing to use Git LFS for large binaries, and learn concrete steps to fix them. You will also practice branch-based work—creating feature branches, testing locally, and merging back to a stable main branch—so that multiple developers can work in parallel. A practical competency is to resolve a merge conflict that affects a script or scene: know when to accept one change, when to reimplement in the Unity editor, and when to use external merge tools. This objective emphasizes communication: coordinate who edits a scene file to avoid difficult scene merges. Together, these skills reduce downtime and keep builds stable during development sprints.

A Version Control System records how files change over time so you can recover earlier states and understand who made which changes. In Unity game development this is essential because projects combine text scripts with large binaries and many people can touch the same project. Git is a distributed VCS: every clone contains the full history, which means developers can work offline and still commit local snapshots. This reduces risk—if a build breaks, you can roll back to a previous commit rather than rebuild the entire scene from memory. A concrete example: if an artist accidentally overwrites a material, you can restore the previous material file from Git history. A common misconception is that version control only benefits programmers. In reality, artists, level designers, and technical artists all gain from consistent history and branching strategies. Another pitfall is assuming Git will manage large binary files efficiently by default; without Git LFS those binaries inflate history and slow every clone. The core takeaway is that Git makes collaboration explicit and reversible: you can experiment on branches, test locally, and merge only stable work back into the main branch. How might a branching approach change how your team coordinates scene edits?

A simple, repeatable Git workflow makes saving work predictable. Start by initializing a repository in your project root using git init; this creates the hidden metadata Git needs. As you change C# scripts, scenes, or assets, run git status to see modified and untracked files. Staging with git add selects the items you want to include in the next snapshot; use git add. to stage all changes in the current directory or target specific files when you want finer control. Commit staged changes with git commit -m "Your descriptive message". Good commit messages describe what changed and why; they are the project memory that helps teammates understand intent. After committing, use git log to review history and git diff between commits to inspect exact changes. A concrete example: after creating a PlayerAbility. cs and updating a scene, run git add PlayerAbility. cs GameScene. unity PlayerPrefab. prefab && git commit -m "Add player ability and prefab". A common mistake is trying to commit without staging; git commit will have nothing to snapshot. Frequent, small commits make it easier to bisect regressions and communicate progress to your team. How would you choose between staging individual files versus git add. in a busy sprint?

Staging is the step where you choose which changes will be recorded in the next commit. Git's staging area, often called the index, acts like a photo frame: you place only the items you want to capture. This is important because you may have unrelated changes in your working directory—say adjustments to a shader and a new test script—and you want to record them as separate commits with clear intent. For example, use git add PlayerController. cs to stage a single script, then git commit -m "Refactor player movement". Clear, focused commits make it easier to review history and revert if necessary. A common mistake is using git add. indiscriminately, which bundles unrelated edits into one commit and obscures why changes were made. Another misconception is thinking staging is optional; while you can commit with -a in some cases, explicit staging encourages discipline. When working in teams, disciplined staging and descriptive messages are the currency of good collaboration: they communicate intent and make merges simpler. Try forming a habit of staging logically-related changes and write commit messages that answer what changed and why.

A proper. gitignore is the foundation of a healthy Unity repository. Unity generates folders such as Library, Temp, and Obj that contain cached and user-specific data. These folders should never be tracked because they are machine-specific, large, and can cause conflicts. A typical. gitignore for Unity includes rules to ignore /[Ll]ibrary/, /[Tt]emp/, /[Oo]bj/, /[Bb]uild/, and logs, plus IDE files like. sln and. csproj. The chapter includes a sample. gitignore and a large list of Unity and editor-specific patterns you should include. Create the. gitignore in the project root before making your first commit so generated files never enter history. A misconception is treating. gitignore as a cleanup tool after files are already committed; once tracked, adding a file to. gitignore will not remove it from history. The correct remedy is to remove the tracked file and commit that removal, then push the updated history. This prevents future clones from pulling unwanted generated content. In short: set up. gitignore early, include common Unity ignores, and verify with git status before your first commit. Configure .gitignore for Unity Projects means add unity-generated and user-specific folders to .gitignore before the first commit to prevent conflicts and bloat.. In practical terms, avoid committing generated folders and user-specific files. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Git stores each version of every file in history. That model works well for text but becomes problematic for large binary files common in Unity projects: textures, models, audio, and prefabs. Git LFS is a Git extension that replaces the file contents in the repository with small text pointers and stores the actual binary data on a remote LFS server. To use it, install Git LFS on your machine, run git lfs install in the repository, and then track file patterns, for example git lfs track "*. unity" "*. prefab" "*. png". This creates a. gitattributes file telling Git which files are handled by LFS. After tracking, add and commit as usual; LFS stores the binaries outside the normal Git object store. A frequent mistake is forgetting to enable LFS before adding large assets; those files then enter regular history and are hard to move out. Another misconception is that LFS eliminates the need to be selective about assets; you still should avoid adding unnecessary large files. Practically, use LFS for common Unity file types and verify using git lfs track. The hands-on activity walks through these commands so you can see the pointer files in diffs and confirm the binary content is managed by LFS.

Branching creates isolated lines of development so you can build features or fix bugs without changing the stable main branch. A typical flow is to branch from main with git branch feature-name and switch to it with git checkout feature-name (or git switch feature-name). Work and commit on the branch, then merge back into main when the feature is complete and tested. This protects the main branch as a deployable baseline. For teams, a common practice is to create short-lived feature branches and merge frequently to avoid long-lived divergence. When merging, git merge feature-name tries to reconcile changes automatically. Source files like C# scripts are usually mergeable as text, but Unity scene files are often binary and cause difficult conflicts. The practical approach is communication: coordinate who edits a scene, lock scenes if your toolchain supports it, or assign one owner per complex scene to avoid simultaneous edits. If a merge conflict occurs in a scene file, consider accepting one version and manually re-implementing changes inside Unity, since hand-editing a scene file is error-prone. The key is frequent pushes and clear, atomic commits that make merges smaller and easier to resolve. How will your team structure branch lifetime to reduce integration pain?

Git handles plain text files and binary files very differently. C# scripts are text files, so Git can show line-by-line diffs and merge changes from different developers automatically most of the time. This is why collaborative code editing usually scales well. By contrast, many Unity file formats such as. unity scene files and certain prefabs are binary or structured in ways that are not human-friendly. When two developers edit the same scene, Git may not be able to merge changes automatically, resulting in a merge conflict that is difficult to resolve by hand. The recommended approach is to prevent simultaneous edits to the same scene by communicating or shifting work to separate scene parts. If a conflict occurs, accept one version and re-implement the missing pieces within Unity, or use an external Unity-aware merge tool if available. A practical example: two developers edit camera positions in the same scene and cause a conflict—coordinate to avoid this or reapply the smaller change in the editor. Remember that Git LFS helps with storage but does not change merge behavior for binary formats. The takeaway: use Git's strengths for text, and adjust your team process to manage Unity binaries.
